conflicts.fact: Force exerted by the 80 kg tea sack, and its extension on the ropes
conflicts.versions: Lessons 3 and 4 use about 800 N (g = 10 m/s²). Lesson 6 uses about 784 N (g = 9.8). Lesson 6 also gives extensions of 3.73 m (old rope, k = 210 N/m) and 0.92 m (new rope, k = 850 N/m). Lesson 3 gives an older-rope energy of 0.18 J, which is incompatible with those figures.

conflicts.fact: Which rope stretched and recovered, and which has the higher or lower elastic limit and k
conflicts.versions: Lesson 1 says the new rope A bounced back and the old rope B snapped. Lesson 3 says the older rope has the shallower gradient and lower elastic limit but also 'stored more energy (0.18 J)' because it stretched further. Lesson 6 says a higher k means less energy is stored, yet it asks learners to predict which rope stored more energy. The sequence is inconsistent on energy stored in each rope.

Lesson 3: k = 18,000 N/m, 8 passengers, 5400 N load, compression 0.30 m, in Nairobi. Lesson 6: k = 12,000 N/m, four passengers of 280 kg total, on Thika Road. Both are presented as the matatu worked example.

conflicts.fact: Dataset the Lesson 2 force-extension graphs are said to come from
conflicts.versions: Lesson 2 stretched rubber band, sisal twine and copper wire with 100–500 g masses and measured extension, but did not plot graphs. Lessons 3 and 6 refer to Lesson 2 steel spring force-extension graphs. Lesson 4 is where the steel spring was first used and the graph plotted, and Lesson 6 also cites the Lesson 4 particle diagram which was introduced in Lesson 2.

conflicts.fact: Elastic limit and sisal twine behaviour
conflicts.versions: Lesson 1: sisal twine shows slight permanent deformation (borderline plastic) at up to 200 g. Lesson 2: sisal twine returns at low loads and stays lengthened only beyond about 300 g. Lesson 6 says the elastic limit is 'formally introduced' at that point although it was introduced in Lesson 2.

conflicts.fact: Mass range and increments in stretching experiments
conflicts.versions: Lesson 1: four 50 g masses up to 200 g. Lesson 2: 100 g to 500 g in 100 g steps. Lesson 4: 50 g masses up to 500 g (0.5 N increments, though 50 g is 0.5 N only with g = 10).
